idiom_name: policy engine (casbin::Enforcer) behind a hand-written handler wrapper / policy-check decorator
implementation_notes: There is no dominant C++ authorization pipeline, so the enforcement half is hand-written: wrap each handler - a template decorator or a std::function chain - with one check that asks the decision point and short-circuits to 403, and never let the handler evaluate rules itself. For the decision half a policy engine gives a real PDP: Casbin-CPP loads a PERM model (ACL/RBAC/ABAC, deny-override, prioritized rules) and answers with casbin::Enforcer::Enforce({sub, obj, act}), and its documentation frames integration as adding an enforcement hook right before the access happens - the pattern's split exactly. Hand-roll only when the rule set is small and static: a PolicyDecisionPoint interface with std::function predicates keeps the seam testable.
pitfalls: A decorator applied per handler type by hand is easy to omit for new routes; register enforcement at the dispatch level so an unwrapped handler cannot be reached.
Capturing the subject by reference into an async chain (coroutines, callbacks) outlives the request; copy the identity data the decision needs.
Caching the subject's roles in a mutable global to avoid passing them through breaks per-request isolation as soon as the service is concurrent.
